cues.text: Let us work through the submitted continuous assessment revision questions.
Before we begin, one important caution.
The original archived options are retained wherever they were captured, but the answer key here is provisional, not official.
Also, some of the photographed question stems were paraphrased during transcription.
So treat the reasoning as a study aid, and always check against your official materials.
We begin with continuous assessment question fifteen.
An EFCC governance audit finds forensic workstations without tamper-proof audit logs.
Which IT management principle is most directly violated?
Option A: Risk management through missing evidentiary chain of custody.
Option B: Value delivery through poor customer acquisition and retention.
Option C: Resource management through inadequate hardware procurement cycles.
Option D: Strategic alignment through ineffective business planning efforts.
The provisional reviewed answer is A.
The reasoning given is this: without tamper-evident logs, forensic integrity and chain of custody are undermined.
Think about what the audit actually found.
The problem is not that the workstations are too few, or that the business plan is poor, or that customers are leaving.
The problem is that the logs cannot prove that evidence has not been altered.
Chain of custody means being able to show who handled evidence and when, without gaps or tampering.
If that cannot be shown, the integrity of the forensic work is at risk.
That is a risk management failure, so A is the match.
Options B, C and D describe value delivery, hardware procurement and business planning, and none of those is what the missing tamper-proof logs directly affect.
Now continuous assessment question seventeen.
An ERP supports payroll and finance, but every tax-law change requires extensive code edits, testing and redeployment.
Under ISO/IEC 25010, what characteristic is weakest?
Option A: Cybersecurity and data security measures appear relatively weak.
Option B: Software compatibility remains the most clearly weak characteristic.
Option C: Software maintainability is clearly the weakest quality characteristic.
Option D: User usability is the characteristic most affected by changes.
The provisional reviewed answer is C.
The reasoning: high change effort indicates weak maintainability, also described as modifiability.
Notice the clue in the scenario.
The system works for payroll and finance, so the issue is not that it fails to function.
The issue is how much effort every change demands: code edits, testing, and redeployment, each time the tax law changes.
The ease with which a system can be modified is exactly what maintainability, and its sub-aspect modifiability, describes.
Nothing in the stem mentions security weaknesses, compatibility problems, or usability complaints, so A, B and D are not supported by the evidence given.
Next, continuous assessment question twenty-two.
A mobile learning app delivers and records assessments correctly, but confusing navigation, instructions and submission controls waste students' time.
Which product quality is most affected?
Option A: System compatibility with other educational software and tools.
Option B: Application portability across different learning devices and platforms.
Option C: Functional completeness according to the initial project requirements.
Option D: Software usability is the characteristic most significantly affected.
The provisional reviewed answer is D.
The reasoning: functional correctness does not guarantee efficient, clear user interaction.
This question is the mirror image of the previous one.
Here the app does its job: it delivers and records assessments correctly.
So functionality is not the complaint.
The complaint is that navigation, instructions and submission controls are confusing and waste students' time.
That is about how effectively and efficiently people can use the product, which is usability.
The lesson to carry forward is that a system can be functionally correct and still be hard to use.
Options A and B concern compatibility and portability, which the stem never raises, and option C is ruled out because the app already works as required.
Now continuous assessment question thirty-two.
A product has strong maintainability but weak usability during actual customer workflows.
Under ISO/IEC 25010, what follows?
Option A: Maintainability evidence alone proves final user acceptance levels.
Option B: Different quality characteristics require separate evidence and evaluation.
Option C: Maintainability scores automatically compensate for usability weaknesses found.
Option D: Usability is not considered a software quality characteristic.
The provisional reviewed answer is B.
The reasoning: ISO/IEC 25010 quality attributes are distinct and must be evaluated independently.
Here the point is about how the standard treats quality.
Each characteristic stands on its own.
A strong result in maintainability cannot prove user acceptance, which rules out A.
It also cannot automatically offset a usability weakness, which rules out C.
And D is simply false, because usability is one of the quality characteristics.
So the correct conclusion is B: each characteristic needs its own evidence and its own evaluation.
Finally, continuous assessment question thirty-seven.
A university LMS quality audit finds nobody owns defect triage, environment management or release approval.
What governance issue is most significant?
Option A: Strengthening of individual unit-level test case logic.
Option B: Significant gaps in accountability and release control.
Option C: Elimination of the need for future performance analysis.
Option D: Gradual reduction in the introduction of system bugs.
The provisional reviewed answer is B.
The reasoning: missing owners cause accountability and deployment control gaps.
Look at what the audit found: three activities with no owner.
Defect triage, which is deciding how reported defects are prioritised and assigned.
Environment management, which is looking after the environments where the software is tested and run.
And release approval, which is deciding when a version may go live.
When nobody is responsible for these, nobody can be held accountable, and releases are not properly controlled.
That is a governance issue, and B names it directly.
Option A is about unit test logic, which is a technical detail rather than ownership.
Option C claims performance analysis is no longer needed, which nothing supports.
Option D describes fewer bugs, but without owners for triage and release approval, there is no reason to expect that.

To close this set, remember the pattern across all five questions: read the evidence in the scenario, name the exact characteristic or principle it points to, and then eliminate options that describe something the scenario never mentions.
